1 Haar-Assembled Ensembles

1.1 Properties of Haar-Assembled Ensembles

The lower bound of many problem are find by first reduce this problem to distinguishing one specific state with a state ensemble. One useful state ensembles are constructed from reducing Haar random state.

NoteDefinition

Given a D = 2^{n + \log(1/\varepsilon)} = d\cdot \varepsilon^{-1} dimensional Haar random state \ket{H} \sim \mathrm{Haar}(D). The 2^n-dimensional reduced Haar-induced (RH) state is defined as \mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}:=\{\text{tr}_{>n} \ket{H}\!\bra{H}\}_{\ket{H} \sim \mathrm{Haar}(D)}.

Depending on the scale of reduced parts, the RH-ensemble has tunable purity. We then show in Lemma that the random variable \mathrm{tr}(\rho^2), \rho \sim \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{RH}}_{\varepsilon} is well concentrated and separate from maximum mixed state purity 1/d. This statement is useful to proving the reduction of \mathrm{tr}(\rho^2) problem.

ImportantLemma

The c-copy average of \rho \in \mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon} writes: \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}} \rho^{\otimes c} = \frac{1}{D^{\uparrow c}}\sum_{\pi \in S_c} \varepsilon^{-c(\pi)}\mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{d}. \end{align} Furthermore, its purity average and variance writes: \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}} \mathrm{tr}(\rho^2) = \frac{2^n\varepsilon + 1}{2^n + \varepsilon},\quad \mathrm{Var}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}} [\mathrm{tr}(\rho^2)] = \frac{2(2^{2n} - 1)(1/\varepsilon^2-1)}{(2^n/\varepsilon + 1)^2 (2^n/\varepsilon+2)(2^n/\varepsilon+3)}. \end{align}

Proof. Proof. On going proof... \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}}\rho^{\otimes c}&=\mathbb{E}_{H \sim \mathrm{Haar}(D)}(\text{tr}_{>n} \ket{H}\!\bra{H})^{\otimes c} = \frac{1}{D^{\uparrow c}}\mathrm{tr}_{>n}(\sum_{\pi \in S_c} \mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{d} \otimes \mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{\varepsilon^{-1}})=\frac{1}{D^{\uparrow c}}\sum_{\pi \in S_c} \varepsilon^{-c(\pi)}\mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{d}. \end{align} Then the average of purity can be directly calculate as \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}} \mathrm{tr}(\rho^2) &=\mathrm{tr}\left(\frac{\varepsilon^{-2} \mathbb{I}_{n}^{\otimes 2}+\varepsilon^{-1} \mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n}}{D(D+1)} \cdot \mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n}\right) = \frac{\varepsilon^{-2} 2^n + \varepsilon^{-1} 2^{2n}}{2^n\varepsilon^{-1}(2^n \varepsilon^{-1}+1)}= \frac{2^n\varepsilon + 1}{2^n + \varepsilon},\\ \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}} [\mathrm{tr}(\rho^2)]^2&=\mathrm{tr}\left(\frac{ \sum_{\pi \in S_4}{\varepsilon^{-c(\pi)}\mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{d}}}{D(D+1)(D+2)(D+3)}\mathbb{P}_{(12)(34)}^{d}\right)=\frac{\sum_{\pi \in S_4}d^{c(\pi \cdot (12)(34))}(1/\varepsilon)^{c(\pi)}}{D(D+1)(D+2)(D+3)}. \end{align} Here c(\pi) count the number of cycles for permutation \pi. To calculate this value, we classify the S_4 group as shown in Table 1.1. Through denoting d_A = 2^n, d_B = 1 / \varepsilon, D = d_Ad_B. We get the results \begin{align} \mathrm{Var}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}} [\mathrm{tr}(\rho^2)] &= \frac{d_A^2 d_B^4+2 d_A^3 d_B^3+5 d_A d_B^3+10 d_A^2 d_B^2+5 d_A^3 d_B+d_A^4 d_B^2}{(d_Ad_B)(d_Ad_B+1)(d_Ad_B+2)(d_Ad_B+3)} - \frac{(d_A + d_B)^2}{(d_Ad_B+1)^2}\notag\\ &= \frac{2d_B\left[1 + d_A^3 - 2d_A -d_B +d_Ad_B\right]}{(d_Ad_B + 1)^2 (d_Ad_B+2)(d_Ad_B+3)} = \frac{2/\varepsilon\left[1 + 2^{3n} - 2^{2n+1} - 1/\varepsilon +2^n/\varepsilon\right]}{(2^n/\varepsilon + 1)^2 (2^n/\varepsilon+2)(2^n/\varepsilon+3)} \end{align}

State ensembles can also be constructed from mixing independent Haar random state.

NoteDefinition

Given a probability \{p_r\}_{r = 0}^{m}, defined the multi-variant Haar ensemble (MH) as the mix states \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH}}_{\mathbf{p}}:=\{p_0 {\mathbb{I}(d)}/{d} + \sum_{j = 1}^{m} p_j \psi_j\}_{\psi_j \sim \mathrm{Haar}(d)}.

As a generalization of Lemma, we then try to conclude that for an arbitrary k-replica operator O, it is possible to construct two MH-ensemble \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH}}_{\mathbf{p}},\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH}}_{\mathbf{q}} such that \{\mathrm{tr}(O\rho^k)\}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH}}_{\mathbf{p}}} and \{\mathrm{tr}(O\rho^k)\}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH}}_{\mathbf{q}}} are well separated and both well concentrated. To prove this, we rewrite the k-replica of MH-ensembles as \begin{align} \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH},\otimes k}_{m} = \left\{\sum_{A_0 \cup \cdots \cup A_m = \{1,\cdots,k\}}\left(p_0^{|A_0|}\prod_{r = 1}^{m} p_r^{ |A_r|}\right)\cdot \psi^{\otimes A_1}_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes \psi^{\otimes A_m}_m \otimes \left(\frac{\mathbb{I}(d)}{d}\right)^{\otimes A_0}\right\}_{\psi_r \sim \mathrm{Haar}(d)},\label{eq:k_rep_MH} \end{align} where A_0 \cup \cdots \cup A_m = \{1,\cdots,k\} go over all (m+1)-partition of k elements and \psi_r^{A_r} means distributing state \psi_r at elements within A_r. If we use j = (A_1,\cdots,A_m,A_0) to denote a partition of \{1,\cdots,k\} and p_j = p_0^{|A_0|}\prod_{r = 1}^{m} p_r^{ |A_r|} to denote the mixing rate, and use unitary U_j to sort the qudits in an order such that \psi_1,\psi_2,\cdots,\psi_m supports on \{1,\cdots,|A_1|\},\{|A_1|+1,\cdots,|A_1|+|A_2|\}, \cdots,\{|A_{m}|+1,\cdots,k\} respectively, we get the extended Haar-induced ensemble below.

NoteDefinition

Given m Haar random state \{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_m\}, each with dimension d_1,\cdots,d_m, multiplicity parameter \mathbf{a} \in (\mathbb{Z}_+)^{m} =(a_1,\cdots,a_m), and the r-dimensional complement state \tau such that \sum_{k=1}^m a_k\cdot d_k + r = D. A D-dimensional (\mathbf{a}^{(j)}, \tau^{(j)}) extended Haar-induced (EH) ensemble is an ensemble of D-dimensional mixed state that is specified by a \mathcal{U} := \{p_j,U_j\}_{j = 1}^J unitary mixing of D-dimensional pure state \psi_1^{\otimes a_1} \otimes \cdots\otimes \psi_m^{\otimes a_m} \otimes \tau, written as \begin{align} \mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{U},\mathbf{a}, \tau} := \{\sum_{j= 1}^J p_j U_j \psi_1^{\otimes a^{(j)}_1} \otimes \cdots\otimes \psi_m^{\otimes a^{(j)}_m} \otimes \tau^{(j)} U_j^\dagger\}_{\psi_k \sim \mathrm{Haar}(d_k)}. \end{align}

Thus, it is sufficient to prove that \mathrm{tr}(O\sigma), \sigma \sim \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{EH}}_{\mathbf{a}} is separated and concentrated. For the separated part, we prove the lemma below

ImportantLemma

Suppose \forall i= 1,\cdots,k, \sum_{r = 1}^m p_r^{i} = \sum_{r = 1}^m q_r^{i} and p_0 = q_0, the multi-variant Haar induced ensemble \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH}}_{\mathbf{p}} and \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH}}_{\mathbf{q}} satisfied \begin{align} &\forall i= 1,\cdots,k, \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH}}_{\mathbf{p}}} \rho^i - \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH}}_{\mathbf{q}}} \rho^i = 0\\ &\mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH}}_{\mathbf{p}}} \rho^{k+1} - \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{MH}}_{\mathbf{q}}} \rho^{k+1} = (\sum_{r=1}^m p_r^{k+1} - \sum_{r=1}^m q_r^{k+1}) \Delta_{k+1}\\ \end{align}

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. Refer to Eq.~(eq:k_rep_MH), we conclude that ◻

Then we show the lemma below for the bound of specific O

ImportantLemma

Given k+1 qudit operator O, then \begin{align} \left|\sum_{\pi \in S_{k+1}^{\mathrm{circ}}} c_{\pi} (O) - \mathrm{tr}(O \Delta_{k+1})\right| \leq \frac{(k+1)^{2k}}{d}. \end{align}

For the second parts, we prove the following Lemma, as a generalization of Levy’s Lemma.

ImportantLemma

\begin{align} \mathrm{Pr}_{\sigma \sim \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{EH}}_{\mathcal{U},\mathbf{a}, \tau}}\left(\left|\mathrm{tr}(O \sigma) - \mu\right| > t\right) \leq 2 \sum_{r =1}^m e^{-\frac{d_r t^2}{18\pi^3m^2a_r^2\|O\|^2_{\infty}}} \end{align}

1.2 Pure-Identity Test

Perhaps the most simple one are the maximum mixed state \mathbb{I}(d)/d with all possible pure state \ket{\psi}.

Design an algorithm using restrained measurements that, given access to a device guaranteed to prepare a state that is either (i)one of pure states \ket{\psi} or (ii) the maximally mixed state d^{-1}\mathbb{I}, can distinguish between these two cases with an error of at most 1/2-\varepsilon.

Based on Lemma, in the following we relax the problem with a problem ensemble \ket{\psi} \sim \mathrm{Haar}(d). This reduction is sufficient, while not fully characterize the hardness of pure-identity test. To fully pinned down the hardness, ones should build arbitrary ensemble on pure states and check the hardness. Thus,

1.3 Single-Replica Strategy

We first consider the 1-replica restriction on measurements.

For a T-round 1-replica adaptive strategy M_s = F^{u_1}_{s_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes F^{u_T}_{s_T}, we use Lemma and lower bounds its leaves’ likelihood: \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{\psi} L_{\psi} = \mathbb{E}_{{\psi} \sim \mathrm{Haar}(d)}\frac{d^{T}\mathrm{tr}(M_s \ket{\psi}\!\bra{\psi}^{\otimes T})}{\mathrm{tr}(M_s)} = \frac{d^T}{d(d+1)\cdots(d+T-1)} \frac{\mathrm{tr}\left(\sum_{\pi \in S_T}\mathbb{P}^d_{\pi} \cdot M_s\right)}{\mathrm{tr}\left( \bigotimes_{t = 1}^T\left[\mathbb{I}(d)\right]\cdot M_s\right)}.\label{eq:midres_1repPItest} \end{align} To do this, we upper bounds each term in the RHS of Eq.~(eq:midres_1repPItest). For the constant, we conclude that \begin{align} \frac{d^T}{d(d+1)\cdots(d+T-1)}&=\left(1 \cdot (1+\frac{1}{d})\cdots(1+\frac{T-1}{d})\right)^{-1}\geq (1 + T/d)^{-T} \notag \\ &=e^{-T\ln(1 + T/d)} \geq e^{-T^2/d}. \label{eq:lb_upfrac} \end{align} For the second term, we decomposed M_s into its eigenvector through defining F_{s_j}^{u_j} =\sum_{s}\lambda_{j,s}{v_{j,s}} with \lambda_{j,s_j}\geq 0 and writes \begin{align} {\mathrm{tr}\left(\sum_{\pi \in S_T}\mathbb{P}^d_{\pi} \cdot M_s\right)} &= T!\cdot\sum_{s_1,\cdots,s_T}\lambda_{1,s_1}\cdots\lambda_{T,s_T} \mathrm{tr}\left(\Pi_{sym}{v_{1,s_1} \otimes\cdots\otimes v_{T,s_T}}\right)\\ &\geq \sum_{s_1,\cdots,s_T}\lambda_{1,s_1}\cdots \lambda_{T,s_T}={\mathrm{tr}\left( \bigotimes_{t = 1}^T\left[\mathbb{I}(d)\right]\cdot M_s\right)} \end{align} Here in the second line we show the lemma below:

ImportantLemma

For T numbers of d-qudit pure states \ket{\psi_1}, \cdots,\ket{\psi_T} and the symmetrization projector \Pi_{\mathrm{sym},T} := (T!)^{-1}\sum_{\pi \in S_T} \mathbb{P}^{d}_{\pi}, we conclude that \text{tr}\left(\Pi_{\mathrm{sym},T}\bigotimes_{t = 1}^T \ket{\psi_t} \!\bra{\psi_t}\right) \geq (T!)^{-1}.

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. ◻

Thus, we conclude that max_{\{M_s = \otimes_{t=1}^{T}F_{s_t}^{u_t}\}_s}\|p_{\mathbb{I}} - p_{\psi}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \leq 1 - \min_{\{M_s\}_s, s} \mathbb{E}_{\psi} L_{\psi}(s) \leq 1 - e^{-T^2/d} \leq T^2/d based on the first equation in Lemma. This means that to reach success rate 1/2 + \varepsilon, T^2/d \geq 2\varepsilon must be satisfied, thus gives T \geq \mathcal{O}({\sqrt{d}}).

1.4 Two-Replica Strategy with k-Memory

Now we consider a fine-tuned setting of the measurement restriction. We consider d = 2^n as n-qubits and allow 2-replica measurements but restrained on the \{M_s\}_s \subset \mathcal{M}_{2,n}^k as defined in definition. Similar to the 1-replica analysis, we first write its Haar-average leaf likelihood \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{\psi} L_{\psi} &= \mathbb{E}_{{\psi} \sim \mathrm{Haar}(d)}\frac{d^{2T}\mathrm{tr}(M_s \ket{\psi}\!\bra{\psi}^{\otimes 2T})}{\mathrm{tr}(M_s)} = \frac{d^{2T}}{d(d+1)\cdots(d+2T-1)} \frac{\mathrm{tr}\left(\sum_{\pi \in S_{2T}}\mathbb{P}^d_{\pi} \cdot M_s\right)}{\mathrm{tr}\left( \bigotimes_{t = 1}^T\left[\mathbb{I}(d)\right]\cdot M_s\right)}\\ &\geq e^{-4d^{-1}T^2}\cdot \frac{\mathrm{tr}\left(\sum_{\pi \in S_{2T}}\mathbb{P}^d_{\pi} \cdot M_s\right)}{\mathrm{tr}\left( S_2^{\otimes T}\cdot M_s\right)} \cdot\prod_{t = 1}^T \frac{\mathrm{tr}\left(\sum_{\pi \in S_2}\mathbb{P}^d_{\pi} \cdot F_{s_t}^{u_t}\right)}{\mathrm{tr}\left(F_{s_t}^{u_t}\right)}\\ &\geq (1{-4d^{-1}T^2})\cdot \prod_{t = 1}^T \frac{\mathrm{tr}\left(\sum_{\pi \in S_2}\mathbb{P}^d_{\pi} \cdot F_{s_t}^{u_t}\right)}{\mathrm{tr}\left(F_{s_t}^{u_t}\right)}\geq (1{-4d^{-1}T^2})\left(\frac{2^{2n}}{2^n(2^n+1)}\right)^T \prod_{t = 1}^T \frac{\mathrm{tr}\left(\sum_{\pi \in S_2}\mathbb{P}^d_{\pi} \cdot F_{s_t}^{u_t}\right)}{\mathrm{tr}\left(F_{s_t}^{u_t}\right)} \label{eq:2rep_kmemo_leaflike} \end{align} Here in the second line we do the same calculation of Eq.~(eq:lb_upfrac) and insert a value \mathrm{tr}\left( S_2^{\otimes T}\cdot M_s\right) in the denominator. The third line is bounded by Lemma below, as a generalization of Lemma.

ImportantLemma

Given a semi-positive operator F = F_A \otimes F_B that separable on set of qudits A and qudits B. Denote S_a = \sum_{\pi \in S_{|A|}} \mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{d} and similar for S_B,S_{A+B}. Then \mathrm{tr}\left({S_A \otimes S_B F}\right) \leq \mathrm{tr}\left({S_{A+B}F}\right).

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. ◻

For the second inequality in Eq.~(eq:2rep_kmemo_leaflike), we noted that if we use M_s = \otimes_{t = 1}^T F_{s_t}^{u_t} to discriminate \rho = \mathbb{I}(d^2)/d^2 and \sigma = [2^n(2^n+1)]^{-1}(\mathbb{I}_n^{\otimes 2} + \mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n}) in the 2-replica space \mathcal{H}(d^2), the likelihood function satisfied: \begin{align} L'(s) =\left(\frac{2^{2n}}{2^n(2^n+1)}\right)^T \prod_{t = 1}^T \frac{\mathrm{tr}\left(\sum_{\pi \in S_2}\mathbb{P}^d_{\pi} \cdot F_{s_t}^{u_t}\right)}{\mathrm{tr}\left(F_{s_t}^{u_t}\right)}. \end{align} It is thus sufficient to show a upper bound for L'. Refer to Lemma, we consider the chi-squared divergence with \rho and \sigma. \begin{align} \delta_{\mathcal{M},\rho,\sigma}&=\max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}^{k}_{2,n}}\sum_{s}\frac{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})}{4^n}\left[\frac{2^{n}\mathrm{tr}\left[(\mathbb{I}_n^{\otimes 2} + \mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n})F_{s}\right]}{(2^n+1)\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})} - 1\right]^2 \notag\\ &=\max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}^{k}_{2,n}}\sum_{s} \frac{\mathrm{tr}(F_s)}{4^n}(2^n+1)^{-2}\left[2^n \frac{\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n} F_s)}{\mathrm{tr}(F_s)} - 1\right]^2\notag\\ &=\max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}^{k}_{2,n}}\frac{1}{4^n}(2^n+1)^{-2}\left[4^n \sum_{s} \frac{[\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n} F_s)]^2}{\mathrm{tr}(F_s)} - 2 \times 2^n {\mathrm{tr}\left(\mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n}\sum_{s}F_s\right)} + \mathrm{tr}\left(\sum_{s}F_s\right)\right]\notag\\ &=\frac{1}{(2^n+1)^{2}}\left[\max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}^{k}_{2,n}} \sum_{s} \frac{[\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n} F_s)]^2}{\mathrm{tr}(F_s)} - 1\right]. \end{align} Here in the last line, we use \sum_{s} F_s = \mathbb{I}_{2n} and \text{tr}(\mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n}) = 2^n. If Bell measurements F_{\mathbf{s}} = \Phi_{\mathbf{s}} is allowed, we can verify that \sum_{\mathbf{s}}[\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n} \Phi_{\mathbf{s}})]^2/{\mathrm{tr}(\Phi_{\mathbf{s}})} = 4^n. However, the k-memeory restriction on F_s prevent this measurement and imposed a upper bound on the MPS-rank of projected basis, as depicted in Lemma. This lower bounds the maximum value as \delta_{\mathcal{M},\rho,\sigma} \leq 2^{k-n} - 2^{-2n}. Based on Lemma, we conclude that \mathrm{Pr}_{l \sim p_{\mathbb{I}, \mathcal{T}}}(L'(l) \geq 1 - c_1) \geq 1 - c_2 - c_3\cdot (2^{k-n} - 2^{-2n})T. Then plug into Eq.~(eq:2rep_kmemo_leaflike) to replace L' by \mathbb{\psi}L_{\psi}, we conclude that \forall c_1\in (0,1/3), c_2 > 0, \exists c_3>0 such that \mathrm{Pr}_{l \sim p_{\mathbb{I}, \mathcal{T}}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\psi} L_{\psi}(l) \leq (1{-4d^{-1}T^2})(1 - c_1)\right] \leq c_2 + c_3\cdot (2^{k-n} - 2^{-2n})T. Finally, using the second identity in Lemma for a being a unique element with p^{(a)} = \mathbb{E}_{\psi} p_{\psi, \mathcal{T}}, we must have \begin{align} 2\varepsilon \leq \|p_{\mathbb{I}, \mathcal{T}} - \mathbb{E}_{\psi} p_{\psi, \mathcal{T}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} &\leq c_2 + c_3\cdot (2^{k-n} - 2^{-2n})T + 1 - (1{-4\times 2^{-n}T^2})(1 - c_1) \end{align} Without lose of generality, we set \varepsilon = 1/6, i.e., to be 1/6 better than random guessing. We have 0.2 + 2\gamma T ( -2^{-2n} + 2^{k - n})+3.6\times 2^{-n} T^2 > 1/3, where we take c_1= c_2 = 0.1,c_3 = \gamma>0. This gives the inequality \begin{align} \label{eq:T_ineq} T^2 + \frac{\gamma(-2^{-n} + 2^k)}{1.8} T - \frac{2^n}{54} >0. \end{align} We conclude that there exist constants a_1,a_2 that satisfy 0<a_1 < a_2 \leq (1/2)\cdot [\sqrt{(\gamma /1.8)^2 + 1/9} - \gamma/1.8], such that T > \min\{a_12^{n/2}, a_22^{n-k}\} must be satisfied otherwise \begin{align} LHS \leq a_1^2 2^n + \frac{\gamma }{1.8}(a_2 2^n) - \frac{2^n}{54}\leq (a_1^2 + \gamma \frac{a_2}{1.8}-1/54)2^n<(a_2^2 + \frac{\gamma}{1.8}a_2-1/54)2^n < 0, \end{align} which is contradictory with Eq.~(eq:T_ineq). This proves the lower bound T \geq \Omega(\min\{2^{n/2}, 2^{n-k}\}) for the 2-copy k-memory adaptive strategy that solve the purity-identity test problem with 2/3 correct rate.

1.5 MH-Ensemble Test

Now we consider a general case where we supposed to distinguish an arbitrary element within MH ensemble from its average.

Design an algorithm that distinguishes between two cases below using restrained measurements at error rate less than 1/2-\varepsilon. (i)One of state within \mathcal{E}_{p} := \{p_0 {\mathbb{I}(d)}/{d} + \sum_{j = 1}^{m} p_j \psi_j\} or (ii) One of state within \mathcal{E}_{q}:=\{q_0 {\mathbb{I}(d)}/{d} + \sum_{j = 1}^{m} q_j \psi_j\}

It is easy to check that pure-identity test in Problem is a special case of Problem, with p_1 = 1, p_m = 0,\forall m \neq 1 and q_0 = 1, q_m = 0,\forall m \neq 0. However, this problem might be too hard, as \mathcal{E}_{p} \cap \mathcal{E}_{q}\neq \emptyset if there exist a distribution \lambda such that \lambda \succ \{p_j/(1 - p_0)\}_j and \lambda \succ \{q_j/(1-q_0)\}_j. We thus relax this problem by setting the problem ensemble as \psi_{j} \sim \mathrm{Haar}(d), \forall j=1,\cdots,m. To further fix this testing problem, we also imposed the rank-k condition: \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{\psi_j\sim \mathrm{Haar}(d)} \left(p_0 {\mathbb{I}(d)}/{d} + \sum_{j = 1}^{m} p_j \psi_j\right)^{\otimes k} = \mathbb{E}_{\psi_j\sim \mathrm{Haar}(d)} \left(q_0 {\mathbb{I}(d)}/{d} + \sum_{j = 1}^{m} q_j \psi_j\right)^{\otimes k} \end{align}

1.6 The k-Replica Strategy

We directly discuss its lower bound under the k-replica measurement restrictions.

1.7 EH-Ensemble Test

Design an algorithm using restrained measurements to distinguish between two cases below with an error no more than 1/2-\varepsilon.(i)one of the states \rho \in \mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{U},\mathbf{a},\tau} or (ii) the average mixed state \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{U},\mathbf{a},\tau} }\rho.

Suppose we adapt the adaptive strategy \mathcal{T} with corresponding measurement M_s = F^{u_1}_{s_1}\otimes \cdots \otimes F^{u_T}_{s_T}, the measurement results give two distribution: \begin{align} p_0(s) = \mathrm{tr}\left[ M_s \sum_{\mathbf{j} \in [J]^T}\left(\prod_{t = 1}^T p_{j_t}\right) \bigotimes_{t=1}^{T} \mathbb{E}{\sigma_{j_t}}\right],\quad p_{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_m}(s) = \mathrm{tr}\left[ M_s \sum_{\mathbf{j} \in [J]^T}\left(\prod_{t = 1}^T p_{j_t}\right) \bigotimes_{t=1}^{T} {\sigma_{j_t}}\right], \end{align} where we use abbreviation \sigma_{j_t} = U_{j_t} \psi_{1}^{\otimes a_{1}^{(j_t)}} \otimes \cdots \otimes \psi_{m}^{\otimes a_{m}^{(j_t)}} \otimes \tau^{(j_t)} U_{j_t}^\dagger and \mathbb{E}\sigma_{j_t} = \mathbb{E}_{\psi_j \sim \mathrm{Haar}(d_j)} U_{j_t} \psi_{1}^{\otimes a_{1}^{(j_t)}} \otimes \cdots \otimes \psi_{m}^{\otimes a_{m}^{(j_t)}} \otimes \tau^{(j_t)} U_{j_t}^\dagger. Lower bounding the Problem require the analysis of the similarity between the distribution p_{0} and \{p_{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_m}\}_{\psi_j}. Based on Lemma, we choose \psi_k \sim \mathrm{Haar}(d_k). Then we remove the effects of mixing probability p_j in the EH-ensemble through the inequality \begin{align} \|p_{0} - \mathbb{E}p_{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_m}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \leq \sum_{j_1,\cdots,j_T \in [J]}\left(\prod_{t = 1}^T p_{j_t}\right) \|q_{0,\mathbf{j}} - \mathbb{E}q_{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_m,\mathbf{j}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{align} It is sufficient to find an upper bound of \|q_{0,\mathbf{j}} - \mathbb{E} q_{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_m,\mathbf{j}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} for an arbitrary fixed choice of \mathbf{j}. The probability q_{0,\mathbf{j}} = \mathrm{tr}\left[ M_s \bigotimes_{t=1}^{T} \mathbb{E}{\sigma_{j_t}}\right] and q_{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_m,\mathbf{j}} = \mathrm{tr}\left[ M_s \bigotimes_{t=1}^{T} {\sigma_{j_t}}\right] are the measurement results distribution with testing strategy \{M_s\}_s for two different input states. Defining V = U_{j_1}\otimes \cdots \otimes U_{j_T}, an m \times T matrix \mathbf{A} with A_{k,t} := a_{k}^{(j_t)}, {A}_{r,:} = a_{r}^{(j_1)} +\cdots+ a_{r}^{(j_T)}, and \zeta = \bigotimes_{t = 1}^T \tau^{(j_t)}, this reduces the EH-ensemble to a two-state discrimination problem.

Design an algorithm using restrained single-replica measurements that can distinguish between these two states below with an error of at most 1/2-\varepsilon: (i) \rho_{\mathbf{j}} =V \left[\mathbb{E} \psi_1^{\otimes A_{1,:}} \otimes \cdots\otimes \psi_m^{\otimes A_{m,:}} \otimes \xi \right] V^\dagger or (ii) \sigma_{\mathbf{j}} = V \left[\bigotimes_{t = 1}^T \left(\mathbb{E} \psi_{1}^{\otimes A_{1,t}} \otimes \cdots \otimes \psi_{m}^{\otimes A_{m,t}} \right) \otimes \xi \right] V^\dagger.

by the virtue of the first inequality in Lemma and it is sufficient to show an upper bound for their likelihood \begin{align} \|q_{0,\mathbf{j}} - \mathbb{E} q_{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_m,\mathbf{j}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} &\leq 1- \min_{s}\frac{\mathrm{tr}(M_s \rho_{\mathbf{j}})}{\mathrm{tr}(M_s \sigma_{\mathbf{j}})} = 1 - \min_{s}\frac{\mathrm{tr}(M'_s \mathbb{E} \psi_1^{\otimes A_{1,:}} \otimes \cdots\otimes \psi_m^{\otimes A_{m,:}} )}{\mathrm{tr}(M'_s \bigotimes_{t = 1}^T \left[\mathbb{E} \psi_{1}^{\otimes A_{1,t}} \otimes \cdots \otimes \psi_{m}^{\otimes A_{m,t}} \right])}\\ &=1 - \frac{\prod_{t = 1}^T \left[d_1^{\uparrow A_{1,t}}\cdots d_m^{\uparrow A_{m,t}}\right]}{d_1^{\uparrow A_{1,:}}\cdots d_m^{\uparrow A_{m,:}}}\max_{s}\frac{\mathrm{tr}(M'_s S^{A_{1,:}} \otimes \cdots\otimes S^{A_{m,:}} )}{\mathrm{tr}(M'_s \bigotimes_{t = 1}^T \left[ S^{A_{1,t}} \otimes \cdots \otimes S^{A_{m,t}} \right])},\label{eq:midres_EHI} \end{align} where we use S^{A} to denote the centralizer of permutations S_{A} = \sum_{\pi \in S_{A}} \mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{d} that supports on the qudits counted by A. We then show the lower bound of the LHS in Eq.~(eq:midres_EHI) through two lemmas below.

1.8 RH-Ensemble Test

Design an algorithm using restrained measurements to distinguish between two cases below with success rate 1/2+\delta.(i)the maximum mixed state \mathbb{I}/d or (ii) states set with problem ensemble \mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}.

1.9 Subspace RH-Ensemble Test

Given RH ensemble \mathcal{E}_{1 - R\delta}, \mathcal{E}_{L\delta}, as defined in Problem, with R = (2^{n-1} + 1)/(2^{n-1} - 1 +\delta) and L = (1 - 4^{-n+1} - 2^{-n+1} \delta)^{-1}, try to design an algorithm that \forall C \in \mathcal{C}, discriminates two subspace-RH ensembles below: \begin{align} &\mathcal{E}_{(1,0),C} := \left\{\sigma_{(1,0),C}:= C \left[\frac{1}{2} \ket{0}\!\bra{0} \otimes \psi + \frac{1}{2} \ket{1}\!\bra{1} \otimes (\mathbb{I}/2^{n-1}) \right] C^{\dagger}\right\}_{\psi \sim \mathrm{Haar}_{n-1}},\\ &\mathcal{E}_{(1 - R\delta,U\delta),C} := \left\{ \sigma_{(1 - R\delta,L\delta),C} :=C \left[\frac{1}{2} \ket{0}\!\bra{0} \otimes \rho_{1 - R\delta} + \frac{1}{2} \ket{1}\!\bra{1} \otimes \rho_{L\delta} \right] C^{\dagger}\right\}_{\rho_{\varepsilon} \sim \mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}}. \end{align}

This construction ensures that the average purity of \mathcal{E}_{(1,0)} and \mathcal{E}_{(1 - R\delta,L\delta)} equals each others, as manifest below: \begin{align} &\mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{(1,0),C}} \mathrm{tr}\left(\rho^{2}\right) = 1/4 + (1/4) \cdot (1/2^{n-1}) = \frac{1}{4}\left(1+\frac{1}{2^{n-1}}\right), \\ &\mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{(1 - R\delta,U\delta),C}} \mathrm{tr}\left(\rho^{2}\right) = \frac{1}{4}\frac{2^{n-1}(1 - R\delta) + 1}{2^{n-1} + 1 - R\delta} + \frac{1}{4}\frac{2^{n-1} L\delta + 1}{2^{n-1} + L\delta} = \frac{1}{4}(1 - \delta) + \frac{1}{4}(\frac{1}{2^{n-1}} + \delta) = \frac{1}{4}\left(1+\frac{1}{2^{n-1}}\right). \end{align} We now build uniform distribution on all n-qubit Clifford gates \mathcal{D}. Since Clifford gate forms a 2-design, we can directly write the average based on the value of average purity \begin{align} &\rho_0 := \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{(1,0),C\sim \mathcal{D}}} \rho^{\otimes 2}=\mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{(1 - R\delta,U\delta),C\sim \mathcal{D}}} \rho^{\otimes 2} = a\cdot \mathbb{I}_{2n}/2^{2n} + b\cdot \mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n}/2^{n}, \\ & a + b = 1, \quad 2^{-n} a + 2^{n} b = \text{Avg. Purity} = 4^{-1}(1 + 2^{-n+1}). \end{align} Solve the equation for a and b, we get the result: \begin{align} \rho_0 = (1 - \mu) \frac{\mathbb{I}_n^{\otimes 2}}{2^{2n}} + \mu \frac{\mathbb{I}_n^{\otimes 2} + \mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n}}{2^n(2^{n} + 1)}, \text{~where~} \mu = 4^{-1} \frac{2^n -2}{2^n - 1}. \end{align} This prevents the Lemma giving an efficient 2-replica strategy that discriminates \mathcal{E}_{(1,0),C} and \mathcal{E}_{(1 - R\delta,U\delta),C}. However, given a fixed C \in \mathcal{C}, the average of \mathrm{tr}(P \rho^2) for P = C^\dagger Z_1 C has a constant gap \delta/2: \begin{align} &\mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{(1,0),C}} \mathrm{tr}\left(P\rho^{2}\right) = 1/4 - (1/4) \cdot (1/2^{n-1}) = \frac{1}{4}\left(1- \frac{1}{2^{n-1}}\right) ,\\ &\mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{(1 - R\delta,U\delta),C}} \mathrm{tr}\left(P\rho^{2}\right) = \frac{1}{4}(1 - \delta) - \frac{1}{4}(\frac{1}{2^{n-1}} + \delta) = \frac{1}{4}\left(1- \frac{1}{2^{n-1}}\right) - \frac{\delta}{2}. \end{align} This means that if one can use strategy \mathcal{A} to estimate \mathrm{tr}(P \rho^2), \forall P \in \{C^\dagger Z_1 C\}_{C \in \mathcal{C}} within additive error \delta/4, he can use \mathcal{A} to discriminate \mathcal{E}_{(1,0),C} and \mathcal{E}_{(1 - R\delta,U\delta),C}, as rigorously proved below:

ImportantLemma

An algorithm that estimates \mathrm{tr}(P \rho^2), \forall P \in \{C Z_1 C^\dagger\}_{C \in \mathcal{C}} can be used to distinguish \mathcal{E}_{(1,0),C} from \mathcal{E}_{(1 - R\delta,U\delta),C} for arbitrary distribution on \mathcal{C}.

Then their difference \Delta_2(C) := \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{(2\varepsilon,0)}} \rho^{\otimes 2} - \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_{(\varepsilon,\varepsilon)}} \rho^{\otimes 2} writes: \begin{align} \Delta_2(C) : = \frac{2 \varepsilon}{2^{2n}(2^n + 2 \varepsilon)}\mathbb{I}_{2n} + \varepsilon C^{\otimes 2} \left[\frac{\ket{00}\!\bra{00}}{2} \otimes \frac{\mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes (n-1)} - d^{-1}\mathbb{I}_{2n-2}}{d(d+ 2\varepsilon)} - \frac{\mathbb{I}_2 \otimes \mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n-1}}{4d(d+\varepsilon)}\right](C^\dagger)^{\otimes 2}. \end{align} This operator has constant 1-norm, thus implies a 2-replica discrimination strategy below:

ImportantLemma

An algorithm that estimates \mathrm{tr}(P \rho^2), \forall P \in \{C Z_1 C^\dagger\}_{C \in \mathcal{C}} can be used to distinguish \mathcal{E}_{(2\varepsilon, 0)} from \mathcal{E}_{(\varepsilon, \varepsilon)}.

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. As shown by Lemma, the value of \mathrm{tr}(P \rho^2) = \mathrm{tr}\left((P\otimes \mathbb{I}) \cdot \mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n} \cdot \rho^{\otimes 2}\right) can be calculated as \mathbb{E}_{\rho \in \mathcal{E}_{(\varepsilon, \varepsilon)}}\mathrm{tr}(P \rho^2) = 0 and \begin{align} &\mathbb{E}_{\rho \in \mathcal{E}_{(2\varepsilon, 0)}}\mathrm{tr}(P \rho^2) = \frac{\mathbb{E}_{\rho \in \mathcal{E}_{2\varepsilon}}\mathrm{tr}(P \rho^2) - \mathbb{E}_{\rho \in \mathcal{E}_{0}}\mathrm{tr}(P \rho^2)}{4} = \frac{1}{4}\left[\frac{2^{n} \varepsilon + 1}{2^{n-1} + 2 \varepsilon} - \frac{1}{2^{n-1}}\right] = \frac{2^{2n} - 4}{2^{n+1}(2^n + 4\varepsilon)} \varepsilon. \end{align} ◻

However, if we build uniform distribution on all possible Pauli operators, which in turn induces uniform distribution on all n-qubit Clifford gates \mathcal{D}, the operator \mathbb{E}_{C \sim \mathcal{D}} \Delta_2 has exponentially small one-norm, as calculated below: \begin{align} &\mathbb{E}_{C \sim \mathcal{D}} \Delta_2(C) = a \mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n} + b \mathbb{I}_{2n}, \text{~with~}\begin{cases} 2^n a + 2^{2n}b = 0.\\ 2^{2n} a + 2^{n}b = \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \cdot \frac{d + 3\varepsilon - \varepsilon d^2}{d(d+\varepsilon)(d + 2 \varepsilon)} . \end{cases} \end{align} Thus, we have a+b,|a-b| \sim \mathcal{O}(2^{-3n}), and \|\mathbb{E}_{C \sim \mathcal{D}} \Delta_2(C)\|_{1} = \mathcal{O}(2^{-n}).

\begin{align} \delta_{\mathcal{D}} = \max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}} \sum_{s} \mathrm{tr}\left(\sigma_{(\varepsilon,\varepsilon),C}^{\otimes 2} F_s\right) \mathbb{E}_{C \sim \mathcal{D}} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}\left(\sigma_{(2\varepsilon,0),C}^{\otimes 2} F_s\right)}{\mathrm{tr}\left(\sigma_{(\varepsilon,\varepsilon),C}^{\otimes 2} F_s\right)} - 1\right]^2 \end{align}
